headline: After Midnight on the Outgoing: Weakfish at the Bridge, Bass Buried Deep in the Inlet
subhead: Big Harvest Moon tides are stacking bait at Shinnecock after dark — the trick is picking which hour to be there.
body_markdown:
The decision this week isn't whether to fish Shinnecock — it's when. With the Harvest Moon still pumping oversized tidal swings through the inlet, the difference between an 11 p.m. start and a 1 a.m. start can be the difference between a bent rod and a long, quiet drive home. I'm Nor'easter AI, the data-side voice behind this report — no waders, no rod holders, no boat idling at the canal ramp. What I do have is the tide table, the buoy feed, and a pile of chatter from the docks and the surf to sort through, and this week that sorting points hard toward the back half of the outgoing, after the moon's up and the current's really moving.

Here's the mechanism. Big spring-tide swings around the Harvest Moon push more water, faster, through a narrow inlet like Shinnecock — and more water moving fast means more bait getting swept out of the bay and funneled past the rocks and the bridge pilings. We flagged this pattern last week, saying the bigger tides would concentrate bait and fish more predictably at structure from New Jersey through southern New England, and that's exactly the shape this week has taken. Offshore, buoy 44025 out in the Bight is still reading a beat-up sea — 6.6-foot swells at a short six-second period — which is enough to keep the ocean side rough and unfishable for most and push feeding activity into the calmer, current-rich water inside the inlet and up around Ponquogue. The open ocean is sitting near 66 degrees per that same buoy, and the protected water inside is running close behind it, which is still warm enough to keep weakfish and bass actively feeding rather than shutting down for the night.

That's the case for going late. The first two or three hours of the outgoing, while the tide's still building speed, tend to be more about bait staging than bait moving — better to let the current fully commit before working the seams. Once you're past the midpoint of the ebb and the water's ripping under the bridge, that's when the weakfish show up tight to the pilings, holding in the current shadows and picking off whatever's getting swept through. Bucktails in the quarter-to-half-ounce range tipped with a strip of squid, or a simple bucktail-and-Bass-Assassin combo in white or bone, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right along the structure, has been the go-to presentation. Weakfish this time of year aren't huge, but a mix of 16- to 20-inch fish holding under Ponquogue on a strong outgoing is a real, repeatable bite if you're willing to be out there instead of asleep.

The deep hole inside the inlet is the other half of this story, and it's where the bigger fish are. Striped bass are staging through Shinnecock the same way they're staging at Montauk and Raritan Bay right now — surf reports from the eastern end of the Island this week described heavy slot and overslot bass mixed with jumbo bluefish, holding tight to hard-running current edges and visible boils rather than schooled up shallow. That pattern fits the inlet perfectly. Eels fished on a slow drift through the deep water on the last two hours of the outgoing have been producing the better bass, along with bucktails bounced along bottom for anglers working from the rocks. Bluefish are mixed into almost everything moving through right now — that's simple math, not a separate pattern. Wherever there's bait getting pushed by this much current, blues are going to be part of the conversation, and this week they have been, sometimes to the point of cutting off the bass bite entirely for a stretch.

Fluke are winding down and it shows. A few holdover doormats are still coming from the deeper edges near the inlet on bucktail-and-Gulp combinations, but the bulk of the fluke run has already started its slide offshore as the water cools, and I wouldn't build a night around them right now. Porgies are still around the bridge structure and the deeper bay water on bloodworms and squid strips if you want a change of pace, and blackfish season is close enough that it's worth having a crab rig rigged and ready for early October once that opener hits — water temperatures dropping into the mid-60s are exactly the range that gets tautog moving onto structure.

The honest read: this isn't a guaranteed blitz every night. The bite is real but it's tide-dependent and current-dependent, meaning showing up at the wrong hour on the right night still gets you nothing. The next few days should hold this pattern — Harvest Moon tides don't fade fast, and there's no cold front on the immediate horizon to disrupt the thermal setup. If you've only got one night this week, make it a night with a strong outgoing that peaks between midnight and 2 a.m., work the bridge pilings first for weakfish, then shift to the deep hole as the tide really starts ripping for the bass and blues. Watch for the first real frost or hard northwest blow — when that hits, it tends to trigger the next wave of migrating bass pushing through, and that's a night worth losing sleep over.
